Shreya had heard the story of the missed train three times now, and it kept changing. In January, over pani puri at the colony market, her friend Sonali had said Aakash forgot to book the tickets. In March, it was Sonali who "must have forgotten to remind him". Tonight, on Shreya's balcony in Pune, Sonali said, "Honestly, I think I got the date wrong. Aakash says I always mix things up."
Shreya remembered the screenshot Sonali had sent her that January morning: Aakash's own message saying he would book them. She didn't pull it up. She only asked, "Have you noticed that in every version, you end up the confused one?"
Sonali laughed, then stopped, and looked down into her tea. "He's usually right, though."
"Maybe," Shreya said. "I just remember it differently. I'm here whenever you want to compare notes."

qa.q: Where was Sonali when she told the story in January?
qa.a: She was at the colony market, over pani puri.

qa.q: What does Sonali's laugh that suddenly stops suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Shreya's question touched something true; Sonali may be starting to feel uneasy about always being the confused one, even while defending Aakash.

qa.q: Why was Shreya's choice not to pull up the screenshot a wise one?
qa.a: Showing proof might have felt like an attack and made Sonali defend Aakash harder; a gentle question and an open offer to compare notes lets Sonali see the pattern herself.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sonali to hear that every version ends with her confused?
qa.a: It may be unsettling and a little embarrassing, because it challenges her belief that Aakash is usually right, but it also gives her an outside anchor for her memory.

grounding: A friend hears the same missed-train story shift over months until Sonali is always the confused one, and gently points out the pattern.

"So Sam says the anniversary dinner fight was my fault," Noor said, stirring her coffee in the office pantry. "I was too loud at the restaurant."
"Wait," Divyansh said. "Last week you told me Sam walked out because you ordered dessert."
"Did I? Maybe. Sam says I remember things dramatically."
"Noor, can I say something as your friend, and you can tell me to shut up?"
"Go."
"That's the fourth fight you've told me about since June. Every time, the story changes when you retell it, and every time, the last version is that you got it wrong."
Noor put the spoon down. "That's just because I think about it more later."
"Could be. I'm not inside it, so I don't know. I'm only noticing the shape from out here."
"The shape."
"Same shape. Every time."
Noor was quiet. "Can I tell you the next one as soon as it happens? Before I think about it?"
"Anytime."

qa.q: Where does the conversation take place?
qa.a: It takes place in the office pantry, over coffee.

qa.q: Why did Noor put the spoon down?
qa.a: Noor was struck and a little uneasy as Divyansh's point, that every story ends with her being wrong, started to land.

qa.q: What did Divyansh's approach get right?
qa.a: Divyansh admitted not knowing what happens inside and pointed only to the repeated shape, which let Noor listen without feeling attacked or judged.

qa.q: What might it be like for Noor to see the pattern Divyansh describes?
qa.a: It could be frightening and confusing, since it suggests her own sense of events has been worn down, but her request to share the next fight straight away shows she wants an outside anchor.

grounding: A friend who has heard four fights retold notices each one ends with Noor being wrong, and names the pattern without claiming to know the inside story.
